title: A Tiny Robot Swims With Living Muscles
summary:
Most swimming robots use a motor. A new robot from MIT does not. It swims using a thin layer of living muscle cells.

The robot is soft and about the size of a stick of gum. It has two fins. The fins are coated with muscle cells thinner than a human hair. Scientists changed the cells so they squeeze when light shines on them.

When light hits one fin, that fin flaps. This pushes the robot forward. By changing which fin gets light, and how often, the team can steer the robot and change its speed.

In tests, the robot swam through an underwater maze. At its fastest, it moved about four times its body length in one minute. Ritu Raman, from MIT, said the robot is quite strong for its size.

Machines that mix living tissue with human-made parts are called biohybrid robots. This study, in the journal Advanced Functional Materials, is the first to show a very thin robot like this traveling from place to place. One day, such soft robots might do delicate jobs in fragile places.
why_it_matters: It shows kids that living cells can become part of a machine and might one day do gentle jobs in fragile places.

keywords.explanation: Muscle cells are tiny living parts that can tighten and help things move.
Tissue is living material made of many cells working together.
Biohybrid means made by mixing living tissue with human-made parts.
Delicate means easy to harm and needing gentle care.
Fragile means easy to break or damage.
